s: Congress may "lay and collect Taxes, Duties, Imposts and Excises, to pay the Debts and provide for the common Defence and general Welfare."
Taxes are judged by function, not label.
In NFIB v. Sebelius (2012) the individual-mandate "penalty" was upheld as a tax because it was modest, had no scienter requirement, and was collected by the IRS through normal means.
By contrast, a "tax" that operates as a penalty for unlawful conduct, with a heavy exaction and a scienter requirement, exceeds the power (Child Labor Tax Case, 1922).
Direct taxes must be apportioned among the states by population unless they are income taxes (Sixteenth Amendment).
Moore v. United States (2024) upheld a tax on undistributed income of foreign corporations attributed to shareholders.
United States v. Butler (1936) adopted Hamilton's view: Congress may spend for the general welfare, not merely to carry out other enumerated powers.
Conditions on grants to states are permitted within limits.
Conditional spending (South Dakota v. Dole; NFIB).
The spending must be in pursuit of the general welfare (courts defer heavily).
Conditions must be stated unambiguously, so states can accept knowingly (Pennhurst).
Conditions must be related to the federal interest in the particular program.
Conditions may not induce states to violate other constitutional provisions.
The financial inducement may not be so coercive that "pressure turns into compulsion."
In NFIB, threatening all existing Medicaid funding to force the expansion was "a gun to the head."
